source_text: Aperuit, de qua hic servitute loqueretur. Omnis, inquit, qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati [n201] . Hoc autem ipsum quam vehemens est contra errorem vestrum, quia dicit, servum non esse peccati, nisi eum qui fecerit ipse peccatum; nec posse cuiquam adhaerere peccatum, quod non is de quo agitur, per se, aut actione, aut vel sola commiserit voluntate? Quam etiam ostendit universitatem humani generis non posse iam a diabolo possideri, cum distinctionem facit inter servum et filium, id est, iustum et iniustum? Hic enim, ut se Christus, ita etiam unumquemque sanctorum a servorum conditione separabat: sicut fuerunt et ante Vetus, et in Vetere Testamento, quos in domo Patris sui manere, et in mensa eius denuntiat iucundari [n202] . Totum hoc autem exhortationis genus inepte prolatum esset, si non liberi arbitrii homines conveniret.
pass_a_gloss: He opened, about which slavery he was speaking here. Everyone, he says, who does sin, is a slave of sin. But how vehement is this itself against your error, because he says that he is not a slave of sin, except him who himself shall have done the sin; nor can sin cling to anyone, which not he about whom it is treated, through himself, either by action, or even by will alone, shall have committed? How also does he show that the universe of the human race cannot already be possessed by the devil, when he makes a distinction between slave and son, that is, just and unjust? For here, as he was separating himself, so also each of the saints from the condition of slaves: as there were both before the Old, and in the Old Testament, whom he announces remain in the house of his Father, and are gladdened at his table. But this whole kind of exhortation would have been brought forth ineptly, if it were not convening humans of free choice.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium

pass_b_english: He made plain the slavery of which he was speaking: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). How forcefully this very statement opposes your error! He says that no one is a slave of sin except someone who has himself committed sin, and that sin cannot cling to anyone unless the person in question has personally committed it, either in action or even by will alone. How clearly he also shows that the whole human race cannot now be possessed by the devil, when he distinguishes between slave and son, that is, between the just and the unjust! Here Christ separated not only himself but each of the saints from the condition of slaves. Such people existed both before and during the Old Testament; he declares that they remain in his Father's house and rejoice at his table (Luke 13:28–29). This whole kind of exhortation would have been pointlessly spoken if he were not addressing people with free choice.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
